concepts.name: AIIB: Founding Genesis and Geopolitical Context
key_dimensions: China's proposal in 2013 vs. formal establishment in 2015 — the timeline trap
Perceived challenge to Bretton Woods institutions (World Bank, ADB) and US-led order
US and Japan's initial opposition and their current non-membership status
India's early sign-on as a founding member despite border tensions with China

concepts.name: AIIB Articles of Agreement and Legal Framework
key_dimensions: Signed December 2015, entered into force December 2015 — same year distinction from NDB
Headquarters: Beijing (distinguish from NDB's Shanghai headquarters)
Legal personality, immunities, and privileges under international law
Comparison with ADB's Charter and World Bank's IBRD Articles — overlaps and distinctions

concepts.name: AIIB Membership Structure: Regional vs. Non-Regional
key_dimensions: Two-tier membership: Regional members (Asia, Oceania) and Non-regional members (Europe, Americas, Africa)
Current membership count (~106 approved members) — fastest-growing MDB in history
Voting power allocation: Regional members hold ≥75% of total voting power by design
Notable non-members: USA, Japan — UPSC trap on 'which major economy is not a member'

concepts.name: India's Position and Shareholding in AIIB
key_dimensions: India is the second-largest shareholder after China — a critical fact for Prelims
India's voting share (~7.5%) vs. China's (~26%) — power asymmetry
India as one of the largest borrowers from AIIB (urban infrastructure, renewable energy)
Strategic rationale: balancing infrastructure finance needs against China-dominance concerns

concepts.name: China's Dominance and Governance Concerns
key_dimensions: China holds the largest single-country voting share (~26%) — veto-like influence on special resolutions requiring 75%
President has always been Chinese (Jin Liqun) — norm vs. formal rule distinction
Concerns about 'rubber-stamp' board vs. AIIB's claim of a non-resident Board of Directors (cost-saving innovation)
Comparison with US dominance in World Bank and Japan's role in ADB — double-standard debate

concepts.name: AIIB's Mandate and Financing Focus Areas
key_dimensions: Core mandate: sustainable infrastructure and cross-border connectivity in Asia
Four pillars: Green Infrastructure, Connectivity Infrastructure, Technology-enabled Infrastructure, Private Capital Mobilization
NOT a general development bank — excludes direct poverty lending (contrast with World Bank/ADB)
Asia's infrastructure gap estimate (~$26 trillion by 2030) as the stated justification

concepts.name: AIIB vs. Asian Development Bank (ADB): Key Distinctions
key_dimensions: ADB headquarters: Manila (Philippines); AIIB headquarters: Beijing — common confusion point
ADB largest shareholders: Japan and USA (equal ~15.6% each); AIIB largest: China alone
ADB covers social sectors (health, education) broadly; AIIB is infrastructure-focused
ADB founded 1966; AIIB founded 2015 — generational gap and complementarity argument

concepts.name: AIIB vs. New Development Bank (NDB): Critical Comparisons
key_dimensions: NDB: BRICS-founded, equal shareholding among 5 members; AIIB: China-led, tiered shareholding
NDB HQ: Shanghai; AIIB HQ: Beijing — both in China, a UPSC trap
NDB focuses on BRICS + emerging economies; AIIB focuses on Asia but has global membership
India is a founding member of BOTH — strategic dual engagement

concepts.name: AIIB's Environmental and Social Framework (ESF)
key_dimensions: Adopted 2016, revised — AIIB's equivalent of World Bank's Safeguard Policies
Three core standards: Environmental and Social Assessment, Involuntary Resettlement, Indigenous Peoples
Criticism: Less stringent than World Bank safeguards — sovereignty vs. accountability debate
'Fit-for-purpose' framework claim — lean governance model critique

concepts.name: AIIB's Credit Rating and Financial Standing
key_dimensions: Achieved AAA rating from all three major agencies (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) within years of operation
Significance: Enables borrowing at low cost and lending at competitive rates
Paid-in capital vs. callable capital structure — how MDB leverage works
Contrast with NDB's lower credit rating — AIIB's financial credibility as a soft power tool

concepts.name: AIIB's Co-financing Model and Partnerships
key_dimensions: Significant share of projects are co-financed with World Bank, ADB, EIB — 'complementary not competitive' narrative
Co-financing reduces perceived risk and imports governance standards
Private sector lending arm: Project Finance in the Private Sector (PFIPS)
COVID-19 Crisis Recovery Facility — AIIB's pivot to pandemic response, breaking infrastructure-only mold

concepts.name: Governance Structure: Board of Governors, Directors, and President
key_dimensions: Board of Governors: one governor per member (supreme authority, meets annually)
Board of Directors: NON-RESIDENT — unique cost-saving model, criticised for reducing oversight
President elected for 5-year term (renewable once) — always Chinese so far
International Advisory Panel (IAP) — external accountability mechanism, often overlooked

concepts.name: Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and AIIB's Relationship
key_dimensions: Common misconception: AIIB is NOT the financing arm of BRI — AIIB funds projects independently
AIIB explicitly states it is not a BRI institution; has its own project selection criteria
Overlap in geography and infrastructure themes creates conflation — UPSC examiner trap
Countries can receive AIIB funding for non-BRI projects — Bangladesh, India examples

concepts.name: AIIB and Climate Finance Commitments
key_dimensions: Commitment to align 50% of financing with climate finance by 2025
Paris Agreement alignment pledge — all projects screened for climate consistency
Financing renewable energy in India (solar, wind) — specific country examples for Mains
Tension: Also finances gas infrastructure — 'transition fuel' debate vs. climate goals

concepts.name: AIIB's Lean Institution Model
key_dimensions: 'Lean, clean, and green' — official self-description with examinable dimensions
Lean: Smaller staff, non-resident board, lower administrative costs than World Bank/ADB
Clean: Anti-corruption framework, Accountability Framework for complaints
Green: ESF and climate commitments — evaluate whether model delivers or compromises accountability

concepts.name: Western Democracies' Engagement and Withdrawal Threats
key_dimensions: UK was first Western nation to join (2015) — diplomatic controversy with US
Germany, France, Italy followed — European bandwagoning despite US pressure
Canada joined later (2018) — gradual Western acceptance
Taiwan's application rejected; suspended members (none formally, but geopolitical pressure on members)

concepts.name: AIIB Voting and Decision-Making Thresholds
key_dimensions: Ordinary decisions: Simple majority of voting power
Special majority: 75% of voting power — China's ~26% share does NOT constitute a veto alone
Super majority: Required for amendments to Articles of Agreement
UPSC trap: China cannot unilaterally block or pass special resolutions — nuanced power analysis

concepts.name: AIIB's Role in India's Infrastructure Financing
key_dimensions: India among top borrowers: Projects in urban transport (Delhi, Andhra Pradesh), renewable energy, rural connectivity
Largest single AIIB loan: Gujarat Rural Roads project — Mains-relevant example
AIIB funding complements but does not replace domestic budgetary allocation
Geopolitical paradox: India borrows from a China-dominated bank while having border disputes

concepts.name: AIIB and Multilateral Development Bank (MDB) Reform Debate
key_dimensions: G20 MDB reform agenda — AIIB cited as both a model (lean governance) and a concern (China dominance)
Calls for MDBs to triple lending by 2030 (Bridgetown Initiative context)
AIIB's balance sheet optimization vs. World Bank's more cautious capital adequacy approach
Question: Does AIIB's rise strengthen or fragment the multilateral order? — Essay/Mains angle

concepts.name: AIIB Accountability and Grievance Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Project-Affected People's Mechanism (PPM) — equivalent of World Bank's Inspection Panel
Criticism: PPM less independent and accessible than World Bank or ADB equivalents
Accountability Framework (2018) revised — evolution of oversight norms
Civil society access and transparency gaps — contrasted with more established MDB accountability systems
